title: Inversion
theme: Inversion after negative/restrictive adverbials, time inversions, "only" inversions, emphatic inversions
goal: Student produces and recognises inversion patterns that go beyond conditionals — for emphasis, formality, and literary effect.
module_chunks: Rarely do we / Seldom does he + base
Hardly had I + past participle when...
No sooner had I + past participle than...
Not only did + subject + base, (but) also...
Not until + clause + did + subject + base
Only after / Only when / Only by + clause + did/do
Under no circumstances / On no account / In no way + auxiliary inversion

units.title: Never have I
units.grammar_focus: Inversion after negative frequency adverbials (Never, Rarely, Seldom, Hardly ever)
units.real_life_context: You front a negative adverb for emphasis, dramatising rarity or extreme experience.

grammar.sentence: Never _____ such a beautiful sunset.
grammar.explanation: Fronting "Never" triggers subject-auxiliary inversion: auxiliary ("have") comes before the subject ("I"). The structure is "Never + auxiliary + subject + main verb". Compare to non-inverted "I have never seen..." — same meaning, less dramatic register.

grammar.sentence: Rarely _____ such commitment from a junior team.
grammar.explanation: "Rarely" fronted requires "do/does/did + subject + base". Present tense general → "do we see". Without inversion: "We rarely see..." — flat. With inversion: emphasised observation.

grammar.sentence: Seldom _____ a film leave me speechless the way that one did.
grammar.explanation: "Seldom does a film leave..." — "does" auxiliary before subject "a film", then base form "leave". Singular subject takes "does".

grammar.sentence: Never I have been so insulted.
grammar.answer: Never have I been so insulted.
grammar.explanation: Fronted "Never" demands inversion. "Never I have been" mixes fronting with statement word order — neither natural sentence nor proper inversion. The corrected form moves the auxiliary "have" before "I".

grammar.passage: Reviewing the season, the coach was uncharacteristically blunt. 'Rarely have we played with so little discipline,' she said. 'Seldom does a team lose three games it should have won. We've earned exactly where we stand.'
grammar.question: What does the coach criticize about the team?
grammar.explanation: Two fronted inversions ("Rarely have we played" and "Seldom does a team lose") emphasise the rarity — and weight — of the criticism. The coach is using formal-public register.

listening_speaking.text: Never have I seen such a sunset.
Rarely do we hear such honesty.
Seldom does she ask for help.
Hardly ever does it rain in July here.
Never have I felt so understood.

units.title: Hardly had I, No sooner had I
units.grammar_focus: Inversion after "Hardly", "Scarcely", "No sooner" for near-simultaneous past events
units.real_life_context: You narrate two past events as overlapping — one barely begun when the next intervenes.

grammar.sentence: Hardly _____ down when the phone rang.
grammar.explanation: "Hardly + had + subject + past participle + when + past simple". Two near-simultaneous past events: I'd just sat down, and immediately the phone rang. "When" links the second clause.

grammar.sentence: No sooner had we finished the project _____ the deadline changed.
grammar.explanation: "No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple". Note "THAN" not "when" — that's the trap.

grammar.sentence: Scarcely had I _____ the door when the rain started.
grammar.explanation: "Scarcely had I shut the door when..." — past perfect after the inversion. "Shut" is irregular: shut/shut/shut.

grammar.sentence: Hardly I had sat down when the phone rang.
grammar.answer: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
grammar.explanation: "Hardly" fronted demands subject-auxiliary inversion: "had I" not "I had". Without inversion the structure reads as a hesitant assertion, not the intended near-simultaneity.

grammar.passage: The novelist wrote of her childhood: 'Hardly had we settled into the new town when my father announced another move. No sooner had I made a friend than I was packing again. By twelve I had lived in seven houses and counted only my books as steady company.'
grammar.question: How frequently did the family move?
grammar.answer: very often (or "every time she made a friend" or "many times — seven houses by age 12")
grammar.explanation: Two stacked inversions ("Hardly had we settled... No sooner had I made a friend") dramatise the rapid succession of moves. The structures are narrative engines for back-to-back events.

listening_speaking.text: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
No sooner had we left than it started raining.
Scarcely had he spoken when she walked out.
Hardly had I closed my eyes when the alarm went off.
No sooner had I finished one project than another landed.

units.title: Not only, Not until
units.grammar_focus: Inversion after "Not only" (additive emphasis) and "Not until" (delayed realization)
units.real_life_context: You stack achievements/qualities with "not only" or dramatise late realisation with "not until".

grammar.sentence: Not only _____ the marathon, but she also raised £10,000 for charity.
grammar.explanation: "Not only" fronted triggers inversion: "did + subject + base". The "but also" clause introduces a second, layered fact. The structure dramatises the layering.

grammar.sentence: Not until I saw the report _____ the scale of the problem.
grammar.explanation: "Not until + clause + did + subject + base". The fronted "not until" inverts the main clause that follows. Past simple realisation triggered by past simple cue.

grammar.sentence: Not only _____ he arrive on time, but he also brought everyone coffee.
grammar.hint: auxiliar de inversão no past simple
grammar.explanation: "Not only did he arrive" — past, so "did + subject + base". The fronted "not only" forces subject-auxiliary inversion.

grammar.sentence: Not only she sings, but she also writes her own songs.
grammar.answer: Not only does she sing, but she also writes her own songs.
grammar.explanation: Fronted "Not only" requires "does + subject + base" (present singular). Without inversion the sentence reads as fragmented assertion, not balanced emphasis.

grammar.passage: The award citation read: 'Not only has Dr. Lima reshaped the field through her research, but she has also mentored a generation of scientists. Not until we examined her full body of work did we appreciate how interconnected her contributions truly are.'
grammar.question: What two achievements does the citation emphasise?
grammar.answer: research that reshaped the field + mentoring a generation
grammar.explanation: "Not only... but also" layers two achievements; "Not until... did we appreciate" dramatises late recognition. Both inversions register formality and emphasis.

listening_speaking.text: Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
Not only is he kind, but he's also brilliant.
Not until I read it twice did I get the joke.
Not until then did I realise how tired I was.
Not only have we cut costs, but we've also raised quality.

units.title: Only after, Little did I know
units.grammar_focus: Inversion after "Only after/when/by" (delayed cause) and "Little did + subject + know/realise" (dramatic irony)
units.real_life_context: You write or speak with literary flair — marking when realisation arrived (or didn't).

grammar.sentence: Only after the meeting _____ what she had meant.
grammar.explanation: "Only after + clause + did + subject + base". The cue clause ("after the meeting") triggers inversion in the main clause. Dramatises the delay.

grammar.sentence: Only by working together _____ we finish this on time.
grammar.explanation: "Only by + -ing + will + subject + base". The fronted "only by" phrase forces inversion and signals the sole future pathway to the outcome.

grammar.sentence: Little _____ he know that the offer was about to be withdrawn.
grammar.hint: auxiliar de inversão no past simple
grammar.explanation: "Little did he know" — classic dramatic irony opener. "Little + did + subject + base" expresses unawareness of something soon revealed.

grammar.sentence: Only when I left home, I realised how much I missed it.
grammar.hint: "Only when + clause" requires inversion in main
grammar.answer: Only when I left home did I realise how much I missed it.
grammar.explanation: Both halves were in flat order. "Only when" fronted means the main clause needs "did I realise", not "I realised". The inversion marks the realisation as cued by the leaving.

grammar.passage: Looking back, the entrepreneur reflected: 'Only by losing my first company did I learn what entrepreneurship actually requires. Little did I know at twenty-five that failure would teach me what success never could.'
grammar.question: What lesson does the entrepreneur say only failure could teach?
grammar.explanation: "Only by losing... did I learn" — inversion after restrictive phrase. "Little did I know... that failure would teach me" — inversion of dramatic irony. Both common in retrospective narrative.

listening_speaking.text: Only after the meeting did I get her point.
Only by trying did I learn what I could do.
Little did I know it would change my life.
Only when she spoke did I notice the accent.
Little did he realise the door was already locked.

units.title: Under no circumstances
units.grammar_focus: Inversion after restrictive negative phrases (Under no circumstances, On no account, In no way, At no time)
units.real_life_context: You write formal policy, contracts, or assert firm boundaries with elevated emphasis.

grammar.sentence: Under no circumstances _____ leave the building during the drill.
grammar.explanation: "Under no circumstances + modal + subject + base". The fronted negative phrase forces inversion. Common in safety notices and formal instructions.

grammar.sentence: On no account _____ this door.
grammar.explanation: "On no account + must + subject + base". Strong prohibition. Note the structure persists: fronted negative phrase, then auxiliary, then subject.

grammar.sentence: At no time _____ the company endorse that policy.
grammar.hint: auxiliar de inversão no past simple
grammar.explanation: "At no time did the company endorse..." — past inversion. The fronted negative phrase "at no time" forces "did + subject + base", a formal disavowal.

grammar.sentence: In no way she meant to offend you.
grammar.answer: In no way did she mean to offend you.
grammar.explanation: "In no way" is a fronted negative phrase. Inversion required: "did + subject + base". Without inversion the sentence reads as a half-formed thought.

grammar.passage: The corporate code of conduct is unambiguous: 'Under no circumstances shall an employee share confidential client information with third parties. On no account may personal devices be used to store such data. At no time has this organisation tolerated breaches of trust.'
grammar.question: What does the code prohibit?
grammar.answer: sharing confidential client information with third parties
grammar.explanation: Three stacked formal inversions ("Under no circumstances shall... On no account may... At no time has...") amplify the policy's seriousness. Corporate-formal register.

cross_unit_consolidation: Trigger inversion after Never, Rarely, Seldom, Hardly ever (negative frequency)
Pair "Hardly... when" / "Scarcely... when" / "No sooner... than" with past perfect + past simple
Front "Not only... but also" and "Not until... did" for layered or delayed emphasis
Use "Only after / Only when / Only by + clause" with inversion in the main clause
Open dramatic-irony narrative with "Little did I know/realise/imagine"
Frame formal prohibitions with "Under no circumstances / On no account / At no time / In no way"
Distinguish "than" vs "when" in time inversions (No sooner... than; Hardly... when)
